title: Teething Remedies: A Pediatrician's Guide to Safe Relief
summary: Safe teething remedies that soothe sore gums, and the ones to avoid. A pediatrician's guide to cold relief, gum massage, safe pain medicine, and when to call your doctor.
body_markdown:
The safest teething remedies are simple: a chilled (not frozen) firm rubber teething ring, a gentle gum massage with a clean finger, and a cold, damp washcloth. Three things you should never use are benzocaine teething gels, homeopathic teething tablets, and amber teething necklaces. The FDA warns that all three can seriously harm your baby. This guide walks through what actually helps, what to avoid, and when to call your doctor.

## Key Takeaways


Cold, gentle pressure, and safe chewing are the remedies that truly soothe sore gums, while a few popular "remedies" are dangerous and should never be used.


- Safe relief: a chilled (not frozen) rubber teether, a clean-finger gum massage, a cold damp washcloth, and safe teething toys.
- Never use benzocaine gels (such as Orajel): the FDA warns they should not be used for teething, and not at all in children under 2.
- Never use amber teething necklaces or any teething jewelry: the FDA warns of strangulation and choking, and says their safety and effectiveness have not been established.
- Never use homeopathic teething tablets: the FDA warns they can lead to serious injury, and even death, and its 2017 lab tests found belladonna levels sometimes far above the label.
- Teething does not cause a fever, diarrhea, or lots of crying. If you see these, call your child's doctor.
- For any baby under 2, check with your pediatrician before giving acetaminophen or ibuprofen. Never give ibuprofen under 6 months unless your doctor says so.


## Unsafe teething remedies to avoid


Some of the most heavily marketed teething products are the ones the FDA warns against, because they can cause serious harm and even death.


Marketing does not equal safety. The products below are sold in stores and online, but the FDA and the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) warn against using them on children.


Never use benzocaine teething gels


The FDA warns that benzocaine gels (such as Orajel and store brands) should not be used for teething pain in children, and that oral benzocaine products should not be used at all in children under 2. Benzocaine can cause methemoglobinemia, a serious and sometimes fatal condition that lowers the amount of oxygen your baby's blood can carry. In 2018, the FDA reported that of 119 cases it reviewed from 2009 to 2017, 11 were in children under age 2, and one infant died. Do not use it, even a small amount.


Never use amber teething necklaces or any teething jewelry


The FDA has received reports of death and serious injuries from teething jewelry, including an 18-month-old who was strangled by an amber necklace during a nap and a 7-month-old who choked on beads from a wooden teething bracelet. In a 2018 safety communication, the FDA said the safety and effectiveness of teething jewelry have not been established. Never put an amber, wood, marble, or silicone necklace, bracelet, or anklet on your baby, whether awake or asleep.


Do not use homeopathic teething tablets or gels


The FDA groups homeopathic teething tablets with benzocaine and lidocaine as products that can be dangerous to children and can lead to serious injury, and even death. In 2017, FDA lab testing found inconsistent amounts of belladonna, a toxic substance, in certain tablets (including Hyland's), sometimes far exceeding the amount on the label, and urged parents not to use them. The AAP warns that ingredients such as belladonna and coffea cruda may be dangerous for infants, even though they come from plants.


Skip frozen-solid and liquid-filled teethers


A teether frozen rock-solid gets too hard and can bruise or hurt your baby's gums, so chill it in the fridge instead of the freezer. Liquid-filled teethers can tear or leak, and the liquid inside may not be clean. Choose a firm, one-piece rubber teether.


Two more remedies to avoid:


- Numbing products with lidocaine: the FDA warns against prescription or nonprescription lidocaine for teething. Prescription viscous lidocaine can cause heart problems, severe brain injury, seizures, and death.
- Alcohol rubbed on the gums: the AAP warns that alcohol on the gums is absorbed quickly into your baby's bloodstream and can cause seizures.


Here is a quick side-by-side of what helps and what to avoid.


Safe to use Never use


Chilled (not frozen) firm rubber teether Benzocaine gels (Orajel and store brands)


Cold, damp washcloth (chilled in the freezer, then knotted) Amber or any teething jewelry


Clean-finger gum massage Homeopathic teething tablets (belladonna)


Rubber and plastic teething toys Lidocaine numbing products (gels or liquids)


Cold water in a sippy cup (over 6 months) Alcohol rubbed on the gums


Chilled fruit in a mesh feeder (babies on solids) Frozen-solid or liquid-filled teethers


## Safe teething remedies that actually work


The remedies the AAP recommends are cold, gentle pressure, and safe things to chew, all of which you can do at home for free.


Most teething relief is about comfort, not a cure. Teething is temporary, and no product makes it disappear. These AAP-recommended options are safe ways to ease sore gums.


### Cold (a chilled ring or wet washcloth)


Cold numbs sore gums gently. Twist a clean, damp washcloth, chill it in the freezer, and let your baby chew on it. A firm rubber teething ring chilled in the fridge works well too. Keep it cold, not frozen solid, because a rock-hard teether can hurt the gums.


### Gum massage with a clean finger


Gentle pressure often brings quick relief. Wash your hands, then rub your baby's sore gums with a clean finger or knuckle for a minute or two. Many babies also like to gnaw on your (clean) finger. It costs nothing and you can do it anywhere.


### Firm rubber teething toys


A safe teether gives your baby something to chew that pushes back on the gums. Choose a firm, one-piece rubber or plastic teething toy. Rubber and plastic toys can safely soothe aching gums. Avoid teethers that are frozen solid or filled with liquid.


### Cold foods for babies already on solids


Once your baby eats solids, cold food can soothe gums and offer a snack. Offer chilled (not frozen-solid) fruit in a mesh or silicone feeder, which lets your baby suck on the fruit safely. Always watch your baby while they eat, and ask your pediatrician about choking safety for your child's age.


### Comfort measures (holding, distraction, extra feeds)


Sometimes the best remedy is you. Extra cuddles, a change of scene, a warm bath, or a favorite toy can distract your baby from sore gums. A little extra nursing or bottle time can comfort too. These simple steps are safe at any age.


## What are the symptoms of teething?


Teething usually brings drooling, more chewing, a rash around the mouth, and fussiness from swollen gums, but not serious illness.


Most babies get their first teeth between about 6 and 10 months, though some feel discomfort earlier. Common signs are drooling, wanting to chew on everything, mild gum swelling, and being cranky. Importantly, teething does not cause a fever, diarrhea, or excess crying. If you see those symptoms, call your child's doctor, because something else may be going on. For a full timeline of when teeth come in, see our guide on[when babies start teething](https://blueberrypediatrics.com/health-tips/when-do-babies-start-teething-signs-timeline-and-soothing) .


## Can I give my baby medicine for teething pain?


For a baby who is very uncomfortable, ask your pediatrician about pain medicine, and always confirm the dose first.


Numbing gels are not the answer. The AAP notes that numbing gels usually do not help, because drool quickly washes them away, and some (like benzocaine) are dangerous. For real discomfort, the safer path is a pediatrician-guided dose of acetaminophen or ibuprofen.


- For any baby under 2, check with your pediatrician before giving acetaminophen or ibuprofen. The AAP advises that acetaminophen should not be given under age 2 without a doctor's guidance.
- Never give ibuprofen to a baby under 6 months unless your doctor tells you to.
- Dosing is based on your child's weight, so get the dose from your pediatrician rather than guessing.
- Do not give combination (multi-ingredient) medicines, such as many cough and cold products, to children under 6.
- If your baby spits up right after a dose, do not automatically give another. Call your pediatrician or Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222.


## Do natural teething remedies work?


The natural remedies that work are the safe basics: cold, gentle pressure, and safe chewing. "Natural" does not automatically mean safe.


Parents often search for natural or homeopathic options, hoping to avoid medicine. The good news is that the safest remedies (a cold washcloth, a chilled teether, and a gum massage) are already natural and free. The caution is that some "natural" products are unsafe: amber necklaces, homeopathic belladonna tablets, and alcohol on the gums can all harm your baby, as covered above. Overall, the medical evidence for any single teething remedy is very limited, so focus on comfort and safety rather than a miracle fix.


## How to help a teething baby at night, and how long teething lasts


Many parents notice rough nights during teething, and the same daytime comfort steps work after dark.


Interestingly, one 2025 study that measured infant sleep found no real difference on teething nights compared with other nights, so a hard night may not always be the teeth. Still, if your baby is uncomfortable, the AAP suggests gentle gum pressure or massage, a cold teething cloth, a warm bath, and quiet white noise at bedtime. Discomfort for each tooth tends to cluster in a short window, roughly from a few days before the tooth breaks through to a few days after. If nights are consistently hard or your baby seems sick, check in with your pediatrician.


Wondering if a rough night is teething or something more? Talk with a Blueberry pediatrician.


## When to call your doctor


Call your pediatrician if your baby has a fever, diarrhea, or a lot of crying, because teething does not cause these.


A fever means a temperature of 100.4 degrees Fahrenheit (38 degrees Celsius) or higher. Here is when to reach out:


- Any baby 3 months or younger with a temperature of 100.4 degrees Fahrenheit or higher needs to be seen right away. Call your pediatrician immediately.
- A fever, diarrhea, or excess crying at any age is not teething. Call your doctor to rule out an infection.
- Some numbing products can cause a medical emergency. After any numbing product, call 911 right away if your baby's skin, lips, or nail beds look pale, gray, or blue. Also call 911 for trouble breathing, a fast heartbeat, or unusual tiredness.
- Not sure whether it is teething or an ear infection? Our guide on[ear infection versus teething](https://blueberrypediatrics.com/health-tips/baby-ear-infection-vs-teething-everything-you-need-to-know) can help you tell the difference.

## Frequently Asked Questions


### What is the best remedy for a teething baby?


The best remedies are cold and gentle pressure: a chilled (not frozen) firm rubber teether, a cold damp washcloth, or a clean-finger gum massage. These are safe and free, and the AAP recommends them.


### Are amber teething necklaces safe?


No. The FDA warns that teething jewelry can cause strangulation and choking, including a report of an 18-month-old strangled during a nap, and says their safety and effectiveness have not been established. Never use them.


### Do teething gels or tablets work, and are they safe?


No. Numbing gels usually do not help because drool washes them away, and the FDA warns that benzocaine gels should not be used for teething. The FDA also warns that homeopathic teething tablets can lead to serious injury, and even death. Never use either.


### Can I give my baby Tylenol or ibuprofen for teething?


For any baby under 2, ask your pediatrician first. Never give ibuprofen under 6 months unless your doctor says so. Dosing is based on your child's weight.


### How long does teething pain last?


Discomfort for each tooth usually lasts a short window, roughly from a few days before the tooth comes through to a few days after, not for weeks at a time.
